story.text: What is the relationship between culture and society: does society *have* a culture, or *is* it a culture—and how does conflict (Widerstreit) figure in this relation?

Society **has** a culture rather than **is** a culture, and culture appears as a **Widerstreit** and **Negativsprache** *in* society *against* society: a standing objection that society is not identical with its own cultural self-image.

Within Baecker’s form-calculus, the statement “society has a culture and is not a culture” must be read with equal weight on what is italicized and what is not: the negation (“is not”) informs how the positive relation (“has”) works. The non-identity of society with its culture shapes how society relates to culture.

Culture is described as Widerstreit and Negativsprache: a mode of speaking that foregrounds conflict, reflection histories, and conditions, rather than positive statements alone. Culture keeps alive the difference between how society reproduces behavior and how that reproduction can be challenged, re-coded, or refused.

This also reframes classic debates (ethnology, anthropology, sociology) about “society and culture”: instead of deciding whether culture is the substance of society, Baecker models culture as the **internal critique** of society’s own operations, circulating within society yet insisting on its non-identity with them.

A counter-position would defend the idea that some societies do effectively “collapse” into their culture (e.g. strong national, religious, or revolutionary identities), such that the Widerstreit is largely suppressed or externalized to enemies and outsiders.

Another objection: describing culture primarily as Negativsprache risks romanticizing critique and underconceptualizing the productive, infrastructural, and habituating sides of culture (e.g. ordinary routines, technologies, embodied skills) that do not present themselves as explicit objection.

Title: [[Culture As Widerstreit Against Society]]

question
What is the relationship between culture and society: does society *have* a culture, or *is* it a culture—and how does conflict (Widerstreit) figure in this relation?

claim
Society **has** a culture rather than **is** a culture, and culture appears as a **Widerstreit** and **Negativsprache** *in* society *against* society: a standing objection that society is not identical with its own cultural self-image.

support
Within Baecker’s form-calculus, the statement “society has a culture and is not a culture” must be read with equal weight on what is italicized and what is not: the negation (“is not”) informs how the positive relation (“has”) works. The non-identity of society with its culture shapes how society relates to culture. 

support
Culture is described as Widerstreit and Negativsprache: a mode of speaking that foregrounds conflict, reflection histories, and conditions, rather than positive statements alone. Culture keeps alive the difference between how society reproduces behavior and how that reproduction can be challenged, re-coded, or refused.

support
This also reframes classic debates (ethnology, anthropology, sociology) about “society and culture”: instead of deciding whether culture is the substance of society, Baecker models culture as the **internal critique** of society’s own operations, circulating within society yet insisting on its non-identity with them. 

oppose
A counter-position would defend the idea that some societies do effectively “collapse” into their culture (e.g. strong national, religious, or revolutionary identities), such that the Widerstreit is largely suppressed or externalized to enemies and outsiders.

oppose
Another objection: describing culture primarily as Negativsprache risks romanticizing critique and underconceptualizing the productive, infrastructural, and habituating sides of culture (e.g. ordinary routines, technologies, embodied skills) that do not present themselves as explicit objection.

---

Title: Negative Language And Reflexion Stories

question
What is gained by distinguishing between Positivsprache and Negativsprache, and how does this distinction reshape our understanding of conflict (Widerstreit) and culture?

claim
Positivsprachen count and order statements; Negativsprachen speak in reflexion stories in which each value is defined by its history of acceptance and rejection. Culture’s Widerstreit depends on Negativsprache to make observers and their conflicts visible.

support
Drawing on Gotthard Günther, Baecker contrasts Positivsprache (which works with ordered statements) with Negativsprache (which embeds each value in a reflexive history of how it came to be accepted or rejected). In Negativsprache, every value carries its controversy with it. 

support
Widerstreit then is not just a clash of propositions, but a clash of **reflexion histories**. It moves us from two-valued logic to a polykontextural world, where different contextures (each tied to a subject/observer) generate their own worlds of distinctions. 

support
When Baecker later treats action and free will, he uses Günther’s idea of reflexion histories to give a non-metaphysical account of practice: the “free” act is a step in an ongoing history of resolving and re-opening Widerstreit, not a jump outside conditions. 

oppose
One might object that the Positivsprache/Negativsprache split is itself too neat: in many real practices, counting/order and reflexion histories are inseparable (e.g. legal reasoning, accounting, scientific controversy).

oppose
Another critique: focusing on reflexion stories may underplay **asymmetric** capacities to tell such stories. Not all actors can inscribe their negations into the record; some must live inside someone else’s Positivsprache.

---

Title: Archæology Of Media

question
How can we study the contribution of media to culture and society without presupposing a single, totalizing theory of culture?

claim
An “archæology of media” investigates each communicative event by tracing the recursive and iterative media operations that embed it in morphograms and kenograms, accepting that only partial “boreholes” are ever possible and analysis is, in Freud’s sense, potentially endless.

support
Baecker proposes a media archæology that asks, for each event of communication, action, or experience, which chains of media operations (writing, images, money, law, technical devices, etc.) recursively frame and re-frame it. He uses Günther’s terminology of morphograms (patterned forms) and kenograms (empty places) to formalize this. 

support
This archæology is principledly local: only “Einzelbohrungen” (single drillings) are possible, and different starting points would yield different reconstructions. This matches Foucault’s notion of archæology as tracing positivity and singularities rather than reconstructing a hidden whole.

support
The media archæology is explicitly tied to culture as the double circuit of society: media enable condensation and forgetting of Widerstreit, but also carry the traces that can be reactivated in Negativsprachen and cultural critique.

oppose
A critical stance might find this too text- and symbol-centric, arguing that infrastructures (roads, power grids, logistics, bodies) need an “archæology” that is not easily captured in semiotic or morphogrammatic terms.

oppose
Empirically, the demand to trace all recursive and iterative media chains may be infeasible beyond micro-cases; the method risks becoming a beautiful but paralyzing ideal.

---

Title: Observers As Black Boxes

question
If culture theory starts from observers, how much do we need to know about the observers themselves—and what does it mean to treat them as “black boxes”?

claim
Observers in Baecker’s culture theory are treated as **black boxes**: their internal make-up remains unknown, while culture and society are explained through emergent properties of observations of observations and their recursive stabilization as eigenvalues.

support
Baecker underlines that observers are “unbekannt”; what can be described are only observations and their couplings. The complexity of every distinction is guaranteed by this unknownness, similar to how Luhmann uses the individual as symbol of the unknown future. 

support
Emergence and recursion handle what cannot be reduced back to observer psychology. Emergent properties of observation-of-observation (e.g. institutions, styles, codes) form relatively stable eigenvalues that observers can test for continued attractiveness.

support
This stance resists ontological cravings to “name horse and rider” everywhere. Instead of filling black boxes with substance, the theory explores how every “white-box” description (clear structure) disintegrates into black-box complexity when examined.

oppose
One criticism: black-boxing observers risks reproducing existing blind spots regarding embodiment, gender, race, class, and other axes that strongly shape what distinctions are even available.

oppose
Another: in practical contexts (therapy, pedagogy, politics) we often must risk white-boxing observers (making claims about motives, desires, traumas). A culture theory that insists too strongly on black boxes may be ill-suited for such interventionist practices.

---

Title: The Whole Of Society As Ecological Form

question
How can we think “the whole of society” without falling back into cosmological totalities that hierarchically order their parts?

claim
“The whole of society” is not an all-encompassing cosmos but an **ecologically qualified** outside to every social form: a conceptual device that prevents premature isolation of phenomena and keeps their networked relations in view.

support
Baecker places “society” twice: as a further observer among others, and as one empirical stand-in for the unmarked side of forms, i.e. for the unbounded recursion of observation-relations. To handle this, he reworks the classical idea of a “whole” into an ecological figure rather than a cosmic container.

support
Following Comte, the whole is a **methodological** safeguard: it reminds the analyst not to isolate phenomena too quickly but to track their linkages in time (predecessors, successors) and in structure (simultaneous relations). The path is from known to unknown, not from part to whole. 

support
With Luhmann, society is then defined operationally: knowing that one is observed while knowing that others’ observations only matter insofar as one observes them. The “whole” is the moment when inside/outside of a situation become thematized as form of society itself. 

oppose
A critic might argue that this “ecological whole” still smuggles in a latent totality: the very idea of “society” as horizon may homogenize heterogeneous, incommensurable worlds (e.g. colonial differences, digital vs. analogue life-worlds).

oppose
Others could claim that certain phenomena (e.g. global capitalism, climate crisis) do require something closer to a cosmological whole, since their systemic effects overwhelm local ecologies.

---

Title: Autopoiesis Of Society In The Medium Of Games

question
In what sense is society autopoietic, and why does Baecker propose “games” as the medium in which this autopoiesis occurs—especially in view of a possible “next society”?

claim
Society can be described as an autopoietic system that reproduces itself in the medium of its **games**: structured forms of interaction that acquire recursive eigenvalue in a network, potentially pointing toward a “next society” organized as a network of games rather than by older differentiation forms.

support
Baecker takes up Maturana/Varela’s and Luhmann’s concept of autopoiesis but suspends commitments to particular differentiation forms (strata, center/periphery, function systems). Instead, he focuses on which “games” within this autopoiesis gain recursive weight.

How can we study the contribution of media to culture and society without presupposing a single, totalizing theory of culture?

claim
An “archæology of media” investigates each communicative event by tracing the recursive and iterative media operations that embed it in morphograms and kenograms, accepting that only partial “boreholes” are ever possible and analysis is, in Freud’s sense, potentially endless.

support
Baecker proposes a media archæology that asks, for each event of communication, action, or experience, which chains of media operations (writing, images, money, law, technical devices, etc.) recursively frame and re-frame it. He uses Günther’s terminology of morphograms (patterned forms) and kenograms (empty places) to formalize this. 

support
This archæology is principledly local: only “Einzelbohrungen” (single drillings) are possible, and different starting points would yield different reconstructions. This matches Foucault’s notion of archæology as tracing positivity and singularities rather than reconstructing a hidden whole.

support
The media archæology is explicitly tied to culture as the double circuit of society: media enable condensation and forgetting of Widerstreit, but also carry the traces that can be reactivated in Negativsprachen and cultural critique.

oppose
A critical stance might find this too text- and symbol-centric, arguing that infrastructures (roads, power grids, logistics, bodies) need an “archæology” that is not easily captured in semiotic or morphogrammatic terms.

oppose
Empirically, the demand to trace all recursive and iterative media chains may be infeasible beyond micro-cases; the method risks becoming a beautiful but paralyzing ideal.

---

Title: Observers As Black Boxes

question
If culture theory starts from observers, how much do we need to know about the observers themselves—and what does it mean to treat them as “black boxes”?

claim
Observers in Baecker’s culture theory are treated as **black boxes**: their internal make-up remains unknown, while culture and society are explained through emergent properties of observations of observations and their recursive stabilization as eigenvalues.

support
Baecker underlines that observers are “unbekannt”; what can be described are only observations and their couplings. The complexity of every distinction is guaranteed by this unknownness, similar to how Luhmann uses the individual as symbol of the unknown future. 

support
Emergence and recursion handle what cannot be reduced back to observer psychology. Emergent properties of observation-of-observation (e.g. institutions, styles, codes) form relatively stable eigenvalues that observers can test for continued attractiveness.

support
This stance resists ontological cravings to “name horse and rider” everywhere. Instead of filling black boxes with substance, the theory explores how every “white-box” description (clear structure) disintegrates into black-box complexity when examined.

oppose
One criticism: black-boxing observers risks reproducing existing blind spots regarding embodiment, gender, race, class, and other axes that strongly shape what distinctions are even available.

oppose
Another: in practical contexts (therapy, pedagogy, politics) we often must risk white-boxing observers (making claims about motives, desires, traumas). A culture theory that insists too strongly on black boxes may be ill-suited for such interventionist practices.

---

Title: The Whole Of Society As Ecological Form

question
How can we think “the whole of society” without falling back into cosmological totalities that hierarchically order their parts?

claim
“The whole of society” is not an all-encompassing cosmos but an **ecologically qualified** outside to every social form: a conceptual device that prevents premature isolation of phenomena and keeps their networked relations in view.

support
Baecker places “society” twice: as a further observer among others, and as one empirical stand-in for the unmarked side of forms, i.e. for the unbounded recursion of observation-relations. To handle this, he reworks the classical idea of a “whole” into an ecological figure rather than a cosmic container.

support
Following Comte, the whole is a **methodological** safeguard: it reminds the analyst not to isolate phenomena too quickly but to track their linkages in time (predecessors, successors) and in structure (simultaneous relations). The path is from known to unknown, not from part to whole. 

support
With Luhmann, society is then defined operationally: knowing that one is observed while knowing that others’ observations only matter insofar as one observes them. The “whole” is the moment when inside/outside of a situation become thematized as form of society itself. 

oppose
A critic might argue that this “ecological whole” still smuggles in a latent totality: the very idea of “society” as horizon may homogenize heterogeneous, incommensurable worlds (e.g. colonial differences, digital vs. analogue life-worlds).

oppose
Others could claim that certain phenomena (e.g. global capitalism, climate crisis) do require something closer to a cosmological whole, since their systemic effects overwhelm local ecologies.

---

Title: [[Autopoiesis Of Society In The Medium Of Games]]

question
In what sense is society autopoietic, and why does Baecker propose “games” as the medium in which this autopoiesis occurs—especially in view of a possible “next society”?

claim
Society can be described as an autopoietic system that reproduces itself in the medium of its **games**: structured forms of interaction that acquire recursive eigenvalue in a network, potentially pointing toward a “next society” organized as a network of games rather than by older differentiation forms.

support
Baecker takes up Maturana/Varela’s and Luhmann’s concept of autopoiesis but suspends commitments to particular differentiation forms (strata, center/periphery, function systems). Instead, he focuses on which “games” within this autopoiesis gain recursive weight.

item.text:
support
Within Baecker’s form-calculus, the statement “society has a culture and is not a culture” must be read with equal weight on what is italicized and what is not: the negation (“is not”) informs how the positive relation (“has”) works. The non-identity of society with its culture shapes how society relates to culture. 

support
Culture is described as Widerstreit and Negativsprache: a mode of speaking that foregrounds conflict, reflection histories, and conditions, rather than positive statements alone. Culture keeps alive the difference between how society reproduces behavior and how that reproduction can be challenged, re-coded, or refused.

support
This also reframes classic debates (ethnology, anthropology, sociology) about “society and culture”: instead of deciding whether culture is the substance of society, Baecker models culture as the **internal critique** of society’s own operations, circulating within society yet insisting on its non-identity with them. 

oppose
A counter-position would defend the idea that some societies do effectively “collapse” into their culture (e.g. strong national, religious, or revolutionary identities), such that the Widerstreit is largely suppressed or externalized to enemies and outsiders.

oppose
Another objection: describing culture primarily as Negativsprache risks romanticizing critique and underconceptualizing the productive, infrastructural, and habituating sides of culture (e.g. ordinary routines, technologies, embodied skills) that do not present themselves as explicit objection.

---

Title: Negative Language And Reflexion Stories

question
What is gained by distinguishing between Positivsprache and Negativsprache, and how does this distinction reshape our understanding of conflict (Widerstreit) and culture?

claim
Positivsprachen count and order statements; Negativsprachen speak in reflexion stories in which each value is defined by its history of acceptance and rejection. Culture’s Widerstreit depends on Negativsprache to make observers and their conflicts visible.

support
Drawing on Gotthard Günther, Baecker contrasts Positivsprache (which works with ordered statements) with Negativsprache (which embeds each value in a reflexive history of how it came to be accepted or rejected). In Negativsprache, every value carries its controversy with it. 

support
Widerstreit then is not just a clash of propositions, but a clash of **reflexion histories**. It moves us from two-valued logic to a polykontextural world, where different contextures (each tied to a subject/observer) generate their own worlds of distinctions. 

support
When Baecker later treats action and free will, he uses Günther’s idea of reflexion histories to give a non-metaphysical account of practice: the “free” act is a step in an ongoing history of resolving and re-opening Widerstreit, not a jump outside conditions. 

oppose
One might object that the Positivsprache/Negativsprache split is itself too neat: in many real practices, counting/order and reflexion histories are inseparable (e.g. legal reasoning, accounting, scientific controversy).

oppose
Another critique: focusing on reflexion stories may underplay **asymmetric** capacities to tell such stories. Not all actors can inscribe their negations into the record; some must live inside someone else’s Positivsprache.
